title: Build a GPT from scratch
summary: Turn text into next-token training examples, mask attention so tokens only look back, stack pre-LN blocks with a tied output head, train with AdamW and a cosine schedule, then sample.
outcomes: Explain why a GPT trains on every position of a sequence at once and why the causal mask is required
Trace tensor shapes through causal self-attention and the full GPT forward pass
Compute GPT-2 small's 124M parameters from its configuration and say where they live
Choose initialization, AdamW and warmup plus cosine schedule settings and explain what each one prevents
Predict how temperature and top-k reshape the next-token distribution during sampling

lessons.title: Next-token prediction: turning raw text into training examples

blocks.md: A **GPT** (Generative Pre-trained Transformer) is a decoder-only Transformer trained on one task: given the tokens so far, predict the next one. GPT-1 states the objective as maximizing the log-probability of each token $u_i$ given the $k$ tokens before it, where $k$ is the context window. Nothing else is needed for pretraining: no labels, no encoder, no second sequence.

blocks.caption: Equation 1 of the GPT-1 paper. Theta are the network weights; training pushes up the probability of every actual next token in the corpus.

blocks.md: We will build the model the way nanoGPT and Karpathy's *Let's build GPT* lecture do, on **Tiny Shakespeare**: 1,115,394 characters with 65 distinct characters. To keep the numbers small we tokenize at the character level: sort the 65 characters and map each to its index (newline is 0, space is 1, `F` is 18, `i` is 47). The first 90% is the training split (1,003,854 tokens), the last 10% is validation (111,540). GPT-2 instead uses byte-level BPE with 50,257 tokens; nothing else in the recipe changes.

blocks.title: One chunk of 9 characters holds 8 training examples

scenes.caption: Take block_size + 1 = 9 characters from a random offset ('First Cit', sp is a space). x is the first 8 ids, y is the same ids shifted left by one.
Position 0: context is just 'F' (18) and the target is 'i' (47). The model must learn to predict from a single character.
Position 3: context is 'Firs' (18 47 56 57) and the target is 't' (58). Same tensors, a longer context.
Position 7: all 8 inputs are context and the target is 't' (58). One forward pass scores all 8 predictions at once, each seeing only its own prefix.

blocks.md: A batch stacks `batch_size` such chunks into two integer tensors of shape $(B,T)$. Every one of the $B \times T$ positions is a prediction with its own target, so the nanoGPT Shakespeare config (batch 64, block 256) trains on 16,384 next-character predictions per step. This parallelism is why Transformers train so much faster than models that must step through a sequence.

blocks.code:
data = torch.tensor(encode(text), dtype=torch.long)
n = int(0.9 * len(data))
train_data, val_data = data[:n], data[n:]

def get_batch(split):
    data = train_data if split == 'train' else val_data
    ix = torch.randint(len(data) - block_size, (batch_size,))
    x = torch.stack([data[i:i+block_size] for i in ix])
    y = torch.stack([data[i+1:i+block_size+1] for i in ix])
    return x, y   # both (batch_size, block_size)
blocks.caption: Data loading from the lecture's gpt.py: random offsets, targets are inputs shifted by one.

blocks.md: The model outputs **logits**: one unnormalized score per vocabulary entry at every position, shape $(B,T,V)$. Softmax turns each row into a distribution, and the loss is the average **cross-entropy**, the negative log-probability assigned to the true next token.

blocks.caption: z is the logit vector at one position, y the target id. nanoGPT computes this with F.cross_entropy on logits flattened to (B*T, V).

blocks.prompt: Before any training, the weights are small random numbers, so logits are close to zero at every position. What loss should the first evaluation print for the 65-character model?
blocks.reveal:
Near-zero logits give a near-uniform softmax, so every target gets probability about $1/65$ and the loss is $-\ln(1/65)=\ln 65 \approx 4.17$. For GPT-2's 50,257 tokens it is $\ln 50257 \approx 10.82$.

This is a free sanity check: a first loss far above $\ln V$ means the initialization is producing confident wrong guesses, which wastes the first part of training.

blocks.title: Cross-entropy is minus the log-probability of the target

scenes.caption: Untrained: uniform over 65 characters gives p = 0.015 and loss ln 65 = 4.17.
Halfway confident: p = 0.5 gives loss ln 2 = 0.69. The loss falls fast as probability climbs from tiny values.
Confident and right: p = 0.9 gives loss 0.11. Loss only reaches 0 if the model puts all mass on the target, which real text never allows.

blocks.md: Training is **teacher forcing on every position in parallel**: the true previous tokens are always the context, and all $B \times T$ predictions are scored in one pass. Generation is the opposite, one token at a time feeding its own outputs back in.

`block_size` is the **maximum** context, not the only context. Because position $t$ in each chunk sees only $t+1$ tokens, the model is trained on every context length from 1 to `block_size`, which is exactly what it needs when generation starts from a short prompt.

blocks.question: nanoGPT's GPT-2 config uses micro-batches of 12 sequences of 1024 tokens. How many next-token predictions does one micro-batch contribute to the loss?
options: 12,288, one per position of every sequence
12, one per sequence
1,024, one per position
1,023 x 12, because the last token has no target
blocks.explain: Targets are the inputs shifted by one, and the loader reads block_size + 1 tokens, so every one of the 12 x 1024 = 12,288 positions has a target. Only the final position of the whole dataset lacks one, which is why ix is drawn below len(data) - block_size.

blocks.question: A teammate's first logged loss on the 65-character model is 27. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The model is already overfitting
The data loader is shifting targets by two
The initialization makes some logits huge, so the model is confidently wrong
Nothing: 27 is typical for an untrained character model
blocks.explain: An untrained model with small weights should print about ln 65 = 4.17. A much larger loss means a very low probability on the true token, which only happens when logits are large and spread out, typically from weights initialized with too large a scale.

lessons.title: Causal self-attention: each position may only look backward

blocks.md: Recall from the attention course: self-attention lets each position build its output as a weighted average of value vectors from other positions, with weights from a softmax over query-key scores. In a GPT that freedom is a problem. Position $t$ is trained to predict token $t+1$, and token $t+1$ is sitting in the input right next to it.

The fix is a **causal mask**: before the softmax, every score where the key position is later than the query position is set to $-\infty$, so its weight becomes exactly 0. Karpathy's lecture builds this up from the simplest case, plain averaging of the past, which turns out to be a matrix multiply with a lower-triangular matrix (`torch.tril`).

blocks.title: From scores to causal attention weights on 4 positions

scenes.caption: Start with every score equal to 0: each query rates every key the same. Rows are queries (the position doing the looking), columns are keys.
Mask the upper triangle (key later than query) with minus infinity. Row 0 may look only at itself; row 3 may look at all four.
Softmax each row. Equal scores over the allowed keys give a plain running average: 1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4. This is tril(ones) with each row normalized.
Now use data-dependent scores (made-up toy numbers; a trained model computes them as q dot k divided by sqrt of head size).
Softmax again: row i puts 0.88 on itself, row s puts 0.53 on F. Weights still sum to 1 per row and are exactly 0 above the diagonal.

blocks.md: Apply both weight matrices to toy one-dimensional values $v = (4, 2, 6, 0)$. The uniform weights give the running means $(4, 3, 4, 3)$. The learned weights give $(4, 2.24, 4.84, 2.96)$: each output is still built only from its own past, but the mix is now chosen by content. Row 0 always copies its own value, because it has nothing else to see.

blocks.caption: d_h is the head size. Adding M before the softmax is the same as nanoGPT's masked_fill(tril == 0, -inf).

blocks.prompt: You forget the mask and train the character model. What do the training loss and the generated samples look like?
blocks.reveal: The training loss drops far below anything an honest model reaches, because position $t$ can attend to token $t+1$, which *is* its target, and simply copy it. At generation time there is no future token to copy, so samples are garbage. A suspiciously low training loss is the classic symptom of a leaking mask.

blocks.title: Shapes through nanoGPT's CausalSelfAttention (GPT-2 small)
blocks.code:
def forward(self, x):
    B, T, C = x.size()
    q, k, v = self.c_attn(x).split(self.n_embd, dim=2)
    k = k.view(B, T, nh, C // nh).transpose(1, 2)
    q = q.view(B, T, nh, C // nh).transpose(1, 2)
    v = v.view(B, T, nh, C // nh).transpose(1, 2)
    att = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) * (1.0 / math.sqrt(k.size(-1)))
    att = att.masked_fill(self.bias[:,:,:T,:T] == 0, float('-inf'))
    att = F.softmax(att, dim=-1)
    y = att @ v
    y = y.transpose(1, 2).contiguous().view(B, T, C)
    return self.resid_dropout(self.c_proj(y))

scenes.caption: Input: a micro-batch of 12 sequences, 1024 positions, 768 channels.
One fused Linear (c_attn, 768 to 2304) computes queries, keys and values for all heads; split cuts it into three 768-wide pieces.
Reshape 768 channels into 12 heads of 64 and move the head axis forward so every head is processed like an extra batch dimension.
Scores for every head: a 1024 x 1024 matrix per head, scaled by 1/sqrt(64) = 0.125.
The causal mask and the row softmax: future positions get weight 0.
Weighted sum of values, then heads are laid back side by side into 768 channels and mixed by the output projection c_proj.

blocks.md: That `att` tensor holds $12 \times 12 \times 1024 \times 1024 = 150{,}994{,}944$ numbers, about 302 MB in 16-bit floats, for one layer of one micro-batch. So nanoGPT normally skips lines 7 to 10 and calls PyTorch's `scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True)`, which can use a Flash Attention kernel that computes the same result without materializing the $T \times T$ matrix. The manual path is kept as a fallback and is the clearest statement of the math.

The causal mask is the only thing that makes this a *decoder*. Remove it and you have an encoder block; keep it and every position's prediction depends only on its prefix, so one pass trains all $T$ positions honestly.

blocks.question: A bug report: the mask was built with `torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T))` instead of `torch.tril(...)`, keeping the `masked_fill(mask == 0, -inf)` line unchanged. What does position 0 attend to now?
options: Only itself, as before
All positions 0 to T-1, including the future
Nothing, so its row is all minus infinity
Only position T-1
blocks.explain: triu keeps the upper triangle, so row 0 keeps columns 0 to T-1 and the model sees the whole future from the first position. The last row is the one that keeps just one key, its own. The loss will look great and generation will fail.

blocks.question: Why does nanoGPT compute q, k and v for all 12 heads with one 768-to-2304 Linear instead of 36 small ones?
options: It is mathematically different and gives better accuracy
GPT-2 heads share their key matrices
It halves the parameter count
One large matrix multiply uses the GPU far better than many small ones, and gives the same result
blocks.explain: Stacking the per-head projection matrices side by side is the same linear map, so the outputs are identical. The gain is purely efficiency: one large matmul instead of many small launches. Parameter count is the same 768 x 2304 weights either way.

lessons.title: Stacking blocks: residuals, pre-LayerNorm, MLP and a tied output head

blocks.md: A GPT block does two things, which the lecture code describes as *communication followed by computation*. Causal self-attention moves information **between** positions. Then an **MLP** (multi-layer perceptron) processes each position **independently**: a Linear layer expanding the width 4 times (768 to 3072 in GPT-2 small, the same 3072 GPT-1 used), a GELU nonlinearity, and a Linear layer back to 768.

Each sub-layer is wrapped in a **residual connection**: its output is added to its input, so the activations form a *residual stream* that every block reads from and writes back into. GPT-2 moved LayerNorm to the **input** of each sub-block (pre-LN) and added one final LayerNorm after the last block. The original Transformer put LayerNorm after the addition (post-LN).

blocks.caption: nanoGPT's Block.forward, line for line. With pre-LN the stream itself is never normalized, so the identity path from embeddings to output stays clean.

blocks.title: The whole GPT forward pass in nanoGPT

scenes.caption: Token ids index a learned table wte; positions 0 to T-1 index a second learned table wpe. GPT uses learned position embeddings, not sinusoids.
The two lookups are added: each position starts as a 768-dim vector that knows what it is and where it is. This sum is the start of the residual stream.
Twelve identical blocks (different weights) each add an attention update and an MLP update to the stream. Shape stays (B, T, 768) throughout.
A final LayerNorm, then lm_head maps each 768-dim vector to 50,257 logits, one score per possible next token.
Weight tying: lm_head.weight and wte.weight are the same tensor. Mapping tokens to vectors and vectors back to token scores share one 38.6M-parameter matrix.
Training: logits at all B x T positions meet the shifted targets in cross-entropy. At inference nanoGPT runs lm_head only on the last position.

blocks.md: Weight tying is old: GPT-1 already writes the output as $P(u)=\operatorname{softmax}(h_n W_e^{\top})$ with the same $W_e$ used to embed tokens, and Press and Wolf showed that tying input and output embeddings lowers perplexity while cutting parameters. The intuition: a token that is a good *input* match for a context vector should also be a good *output* prediction for it.

Count GPT-2 small's parameters ($V=50257$, $T_{max}=1024$, $C=768$, $L=12$, biases on). Per block: attention has $4C^2+4C$ (q, k, v and output projections), the MLP $8C^2+5C$, the two LayerNorms $4C$. That is $12C^2+13C = 7{,}087{,}872$ per block.

blocks.caption: Computed exactly by script. Without tying, a separate lm_head would add another V x C = 38,597,376.

scenes.caption: Tied model: 124.44M total. The MLPs hold 45.5%, the token table 31.0%, attention 22.8%. LayerNorms are only 38,400 parameters.
Untied: a separate output matrix adds 38.6M, a model of 163.04M that is 31% larger for the same compute per block.

blocks.md: Running the same count for the larger GPT-2 shapes (24 x 1024, 36 x 1280, 48 x 1600) gives 354.8M, 774.0M and 1557.6M. The GPT-2 paper's Table 2 lists 117M, 345M, 762M and 1542M; nanoGPT counts the released checkpoints' tensors and so calls the smallest one 124M. nanoGPT also pads the vocabulary to 50,304 (786 x 64) when training from scratch, because matrix sizes that are multiples of 64 run faster on GPUs.

blocks.prompt: You double the width $C$ from 768 to 1536 and keep 12 layers. Roughly how much do the block parameters grow?
blocks.reveal: About **4 times**: block parameters scale as $12C^2$, so $7{,}087{,}872$ becomes $28{,}331{,}520$ per block (a ratio of 3.997). The embedding table only doubles, since it is $V \times C$. This is why width is the expensive knob.

blocks.md: Pre-LN vs post-LN is not cosmetic. Xiong et al. show that in the original post-LN Transformer the gradients near the output are large at initialization, which is why it needs a careful learning-rate warmup. Placing LayerNorm inside the residual branch, as GPT-2 does, gives well-behaved gradients at initialization.

A GPT is just: embed (token + position), $L$ x [pre-LN causal attention, pre-LN MLP, each added to the residual stream], final LayerNorm, project back to vocabulary scores with the tied embedding matrix.

blocks.question: In nanoGPT's Block, where is LayerNorm applied?
options: After each residual addition, x = LN(x + attn(x))
On the input to each sub-layer, x = x + attn(LN(x)), plus one final ln_f
Only once, before the first block
Only on the attention scores before the softmax
blocks.explain: GPT-2 moved LayerNorm to the input of each sub-block and added a final LayerNorm after the last block. The first option is the post-LN layout of the 2017 Transformer.

blocks.question: For GPT-2 small, roughly what share of all parameters sits in the MLPs?
options: About 10%
About 23%
About 45%
About 31%
blocks.explain: The MLPs have 8C^2 + 5C per block, twice attention's 4C^2 + 4C, totalling 56.67M of 124.44M, which is 45.5%. 23% is attention and 31% is the token embedding table.

lessons.title: Training it: initialization, AdamW and a warmup plus cosine schedule

blocks.md: The architecture is done; the rest is careful deep-net practice from the prerequisite course. nanoGPT initializes every Linear and Embedding weight from $\mathcal{N}(0, 0.02^2)$ and every bias at zero, the same $\mathcal{N}(0,0.02)$ GPT-1 reports. One exception comes from GPT-2: the projections that write into the residual stream (`c_proj` in attention and in the MLP) are scaled down by $1/\sqrt{N}$, where $N$ is the number of residual layers.

blocks.prompt: GPT-2 small has 12 blocks, each with 2 residual additions. What standard deviation does nanoGPT use for c_proj weights, and why shrink them at all?
blocks.reveal:
$0.02/\sqrt{2 \cdot 12} = 0.02/\sqrt{24} \approx 0.0041$.

Each residual addition adds a roughly independent random contribution, so at initialization the variance of the stream grows with the number of additions (24 here). Scaling the writers by $1/\sqrt{24}$ keeps the total roughly the size of a single contribution, so deeper models start in the same regime as shallow ones. The GPT-2 paper describes it as accounting for accumulation on the residual path with depth.

blocks.md: The optimizer is **AdamW** (Adam with weight decay applied directly to the weights, decoupled from the gradient step, per Loshchilov and Hutter). nanoGPT's GPT-2 settings: $\beta_1=0.9$, $\beta_2=0.95$, weight decay 0.1, gradient norm clipped at 1.0. Weight decay goes only to tensors with 2 or more dimensions (matmul weights and embeddings); biases and LayerNorm gains are not decayed.

Batch size is counted in tokens. nanoGPT's GPT-2 run uses micro-batches of 12 x 1024 tokens and accumulates gradients over 40 of them (5 per GPU on 8 GPUs) before each optimizer step: $12 \times 1024 \times 40 = 491{,}520$ tokens per step. 600,000 steps is about 294.9 billion tokens, the "300B" in the config. GPT-2 itself used batches of 512 sequences of 1024 tokens.

blocks.caption: nanoGPT's get_lr: linear warmup for w steps, then cosine decay to eta_min at step D. GPT defaults: eta_max 6e-4, w 2000, D 600,000, eta_min 6e-5.

blocks.title: nanoGPT's learning-rate schedule for GPT-2 small

scenes.caption: Defaults: 2,000 warmup steps are under 0.4% of the run, so warmup looks like a vertical wall. Midway through decay the rate is exactly the mean of peak and floor.
Exaggerated warmup of 60k steps to make the linear ramp visible. Small early steps protect the freshly initialized model while gradient statistics settle.
GPT-1's schedule shape for comparison: peak 2.5e-4, 2,000 warmup updates, cosine annealing all the way to 0. Its real run was not 600k steps long, and the fixed markers still show nanoGPT's defaults.
Compare with a constant rate: the cosine run spends the last part of training at small steps, which lets the loss settle into a lower region instead of bouncing around it.

blocks.md: The Shakespeare baby GPT changes a few knobs because it is tiny and sees few tokens per step: 6 layers, 6 heads, width 384, context 256, batch 64, dropout 0.2, peak LR 1e-3 warming up for 100 steps and decaying to 1e-4 over 5,000, and $\beta_2=0.99$. nanoGPT's parameter count (with no biases, its training default, and excluding position embeddings) comes to 10.65M. The README reports about 3 minutes on one A100 GPU, and a best validation loss of 1.4697.

blocks.title: Reported losses in nats per token (lower is better)

scenes.caption: Character level: from 4.17 untrained to 1.88 for the small CPU config and 1.47 for the 3-minute GPU run (nanoGPT README).
GPT-2 BPE tokens on OpenWebText: 10.82 untrained; the released 124M checkpoint scores 3.12 val, and nanoGPT's 124M run reaches about 2.85 after roughly 4 days on 8 A100s.

blocks.md: Never compare losses across tokenizers. 1.47 nats per *character* and 2.85 nats per *BPE token* measure different things: a BPE token covers several characters, so it is much harder to predict. The released GPT-2 scores 3.12 on OWT partly because it was trained on WebText, not OpenWebText; nanoGPT notes that fine-tuning it on OWT brings it to about 2.85.

How much compute is that? nanoGPT's MFU (model FLOPs utilization: achieved FLOPs as a share of the GPU's peak) estimate counts $6N + 12\,L\,H\,Q\,T$ FLOPs per token, where $6N$ covers the forward and backward matrix multiplies of the $N$ weights and the second term covers attention ($H$ heads of size $Q$ over context $T$). For the 124M model at $T=1024$ that is about 855 million FLOPs per token, so $4.2\times10^{14}$ per optimizer step and about $2.5\times10^{20}$ for the whole run.

The training loop is the generic one (forward, cross-entropy, backward, clip, AdamW step), and the GPT-specific knowledge is in the settings: small normal init with scaled residual projections, decoupled weight decay on matrices only, warmup then cosine decay, and big token batches via gradient accumulation.

blocks.question: Which parameters does nanoGPT's configure_optimizers exclude from weight decay?
options: The token embedding table, because it is tied
All attention weights
Nothing; AdamW decays every tensor equally
Tensors with fewer than 2 dimensions: biases and LayerNorm weights
blocks.explain: The rule is p.dim() >= 2 gets weight_decay, everything else gets 0. So matmul weights and embeddings (including the tied wte) are decayed, while 1-D biases and LayerNorm gains and shifts are not.

blocks.question: You start GPT-2 small at the peak rate 6e-4 with no warmup and the loss spikes to NaN within 100 steps. Which change addresses the cause most directly?
options: Increase weight decay to 1.0
Add a linear warmup over the first few thousand steps
Remove gradient clipping
Switch from cosine decay to a constant rate
blocks.explain: In the first steps Adam's running statistics are still settling, so full-size updates can blow up a freshly initialized model. Warmup ramps the step size meanwhile, which is why nanoGPT warms up for 2,000 steps. Xiong et al. find pre-LN models like GPT-2 less fragile here than post-LN ones, but warmup remains the standard fix. Removing clipping or raising decay does not touch the cause, and the decay shape only matters later.

blocks.question: A friend's character-level model reaches 1.3 val loss and a colleague's BPE model 2.9. Which is better?
options: They cannot be compared: one is nats per character, the other nats per token
The character model, since 1.3 is lower
The BPE model, since 2.9 is higher
They are equal after dividing by ln 2
blocks.explain: Cross-entropy is measured per token, and the two tokenizers define different tokens over the same text. To compare you would need a per-character or per-byte measure on the same data.

lessons.title: Generating text: the sampling loop, temperature and top-k

blocks.md: A trained GPT gives a distribution over the next token. **Generation** is a loop: run the model on the current context, take the logits at the **last** position only, turn them into probabilities, sample one token, append it, repeat. This is called *autoregressive* decoding, because each output becomes part of the next input.

blocks.title: nanoGPT's generate on the Shakespeare model (block_size 256)
blocks.code:
@torch.no_grad()
def generate(self, idx, max_new_tokens, temperature=1.0, top_k=None):
    for _ in range(max_new_tokens):
        bs = self.config.block_size
        idx_cond = idx if idx.size(1) <= bs else idx[:, -bs:]
        logits, _ = self(idx_cond)
        logits = logits[:, -1, :] / temperature
        if top_k is not None:
            v, _ = torch.topk(logits, min(top_k, logits.size(-1)))
            logits[logits < v[:, [-1]]] = -float('Inf')
        probs = F.softmax(logits, dim=-1)
        idx_next = torch.multinomial(probs, num_samples=1)
        idx = torch.cat((idx, idx_next), dim=1)
    return idx

scenes.caption: Start from a 1 x 1 context holding token 0, the newline character, as the lecture does.
Context fits, so no crop. The forward pass (in inference mode) only computes lm_head for the final position.
Keep the last position's 65 logits and divide by the temperature.
Softmax, then draw one id at random in proportion to its probability (not the argmax).
Append and loop. After 256 new tokens idx has 257 columns.
Now the context is longer than block_size, so only the last 256 tokens are fed. wpe has just 256 rows, so the model cannot even represent position 256.

blocks.md: **Temperature** $\tau$ divides the logits before the softmax. $\tau<1$ sharpens the distribution toward the top choices; $\tau>1$ flattens it toward uniform. **Top-k** keeps only the $k$ largest logits, sets the rest to $-\infty$, and renormalizes, so very unlikely tokens can never be drawn. nanoGPT's `sample.py` exposes both (`--temperature`, `--top_k`).

blocks.caption: z are the logits of the final position; tau is the temperature.

scenes.caption: Temperature 1: the model's own distribution. A gets 56.3%, but 43.7% of the time something else is sampled.
Temperature 0.5: logits are doubled, so A rises to 82.9% and E drops to 0.2%. Text becomes safer and more repetitive.
Temperature 2: logits are halved, so A falls to 37.5% and E rises to 8.4%. Text becomes more varied and more error-prone.
Top-k = 2 at temperature 1: only A and B survive and are renormalized to 73.1% and 26.9%. The tail can never be drawn.
Top-k = 3 at temperature 0.8, both knobs together: 69.5%, 19.9%, 10.7%.

blocks.prompt: What does sampling become as the temperature goes toward 0, and as it grows very large?
blocks.reveal: As $\tau \to 0$ the largest logit dominates the softmax completely, so sampling becomes **greedy decoding**: always pick the argmax (nanoGPT would divide by zero at exactly 0, so you approximate with a tiny value). As $\tau \to \infty$ all logits divided by $\tau$ approach 0 and the distribution becomes uniform over the vocabulary, which produces noise.

blocks.md: Each new token reruns the model over the whole cropped context, even though the earlier positions' keys and values have not changed. nanoGPT accepts that cost for clarity. Production inference engines instead keep a **KV cache** of past keys and values so each step only processes the new token; that is the subject of the inference courses.

The model never stores the text it generated anywhere except in `idx`. There is no hidden memory across calls: anything older than `block_size` tokens is simply cropped away and cannot influence the next prediction.

Training scores all positions in parallel with teacher forcing; generation is a sequential loop over the same network that samples from the last position's distribution, shaped by temperature and top-k.
Scaling this exact recipe up is how the GPT series grew: GPT-3 is an autoregressive language model with 175 billion parameters, still a stack of decoder blocks trained on next-token prediction.

blocks.question: Why does generate keep only `logits[:, -1, :]`?
options: Earlier positions' logits are always wrong
It saves memory and gives the same result as averaging all positions
Only the last position's logits predict the token that comes after the current context
The causal mask zeroes out the other positions' logits
blocks.explain: Position t's logits predict token t+1. Earlier positions predict tokens that already exist in the context, so they are useless here. The causal mask zeroes attention weights, not logits.

blocks.question: A sampling script uses `logits[logits <= v[:, [-1]]] = -inf` (note `<=`) with top_k = 5. What happens?
options: Nothing changes; < and <= behave the same
The 5th-largest logit (and any ties with it) is also removed, so only 4 tokens survive; with top_k = 1 every logit is masked and softmax returns NaN
Top-k now keeps 6 tokens
Temperature stops having an effect
blocks.explain: v[:, [-1]] is the k-th largest logit, the threshold that must survive. With <= it is thrown away too, leaving k - 1 choices, and for k = 1 nothing survives: all minus infinity gives NaN probabilities and multinomial fails.
